transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit hard to explain, but my daughter suggested I come in. She says I just never stop, and, well, she's right. I'm 70 years old, you know, retired, supposed to be taking it easy, but I feel like I’m always up and moving. Always. Even on what's supposed to be a quiet Tuesday, I just can't seem to sit still. I'll sit down in my favorite chair—the floral one by the window, gets lovely light—and I think, "Okay, time to relax." But before I know it, I'm up. I'm bouncing from checking the roster for my garden club—we're planning the spring luncheon, and Mrs. Higgins is being very difficult about the centerpieces—and then suddenly I'm over at my knitting bag because I remembered I need to fix a dropped stitch on my grandson's sweater, but on the way there I see the travel papers for that cruise we're thinking of taking next year, and I just have to look at them right then. And the funny thing is, I do all this before I’ve really finished any one thing. I just flutter around the house all day long, from one thing to the next, like a bee in a flowerbed, and by the end of the day I'm exhausted but nothing is actually done! It's just... constant.
Have you been feeling more energetic or in a particularly good mood lately, like you don’t need as much sleep or that your thoughts are racing faster than usual?

Oh, no, no, it's not like that at all. I wouldn't say I'm in a particularly *good* mood—I mean, I'm generally a cheerful person, ask anyone at the church bake sale, I always have a smile when I'm handing out the snickerdoodles—but I'm not, you know, overly happy or anything out of the ordinary. 

And as for sleep! Oh my goodness, no. I absolutely need my sleep. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just a complete wreck the next day. I usually try to be in bed by 10:30 PM, right after the late local news with that nice weatherman, because if I stay up any later, say, watching one of those British mystery shows my daughter got me hooked on, I just feel it the whole next morning. My eyes get all heavy and I can barely focus on my crossword puzzle. 

So, no, I definitely need my rest. It's not that I have this... this endless well of energy or that my mind is racing with brilliant new ideas or anything like that. I'm just normal old me, mood-wise. It's more just that I can't seem to settle down during the day. Even when I *want* to just sit and relax, my body just wants to get up and fiddle with things. But I'm certainly not feeling like I can skip a night of sleep. In fact, like I was saying before, by the evening, my feet are aching from all the pacing and puttering around the house, and I am just plain worn out!
Do you ever feel down, hopeless, or like you don’t enjoy things the way you used to?

Oh, no, no, not at all. I wouldn't say I feel down or hopeless. I mean, goodness, there's just too much to do to sit around feeling hopeless! Like I was saying about the garden club—there's always something going on. Even when Mrs. Higgins is being a thorn in my side about the centerpieces, I still love being part of it. I love the planning, I love the flowers, I love the little sandwiches we have at the meetings. 

And my grandson, oh, he's just a delight. Fixing his little sweater, even if I get distracted halfway through, it still brings me joy. I still love knitting, I still love reading my mysteries, I still love going for my morning walks when the weather is nice. Sometimes I think I enjoy things almost *too* much, because I want to do them all at the same time! 

I mean, sure, I get frustrated when I realize I've spent the whole morning bouncing around and haven't actually finished a single chore. Like last Thursday, I was supposed to be cleaning out the hall closet, and I found an old photo album, and next thing I know I'm pulling out recipe cards to find the one for my mother's peach cobbler because I saw a picture of a picnic we had back in 1982. That can be a little annoying, realizing the closet is still a mess. But it doesn't make me feel hopeless or sad. It's just... well, it's just me being me, I suppose. Just a bit more scattered than I used to be. But my spirits are fine, really they are. I still look forward to each day, even if I end up spending it running in circles!
Do you ever feel restless or physically unable to sit still, like there's an inner need to keep moving?

Oh, yes! Yes, that is exactly it. That's a perfect way to describe it. It's like... well, if I have to sit still for too long, I get this terribly stirred-up feeling inside. It’s almost like a little motor humming right in my chest or my stomach, and it just tells me I need to move. 

Like, if my daughter comes over and wants to watch a program—we were watching one of those lovely British baking shows the other day, the one with the big white tent, I just love the pastries they make, they look so delicious—but even though I was truly enjoying it, maybe twenty or thirty minutes in, I got that feeling. I just couldn't take it anymore. I absolutely had to stand up. When that stirred-up feeling hits, I get this overwhelming urge that I need to go straighten something or go check on something. 

I told my daughter I was just going to check if the back porch door was locked. Now, mind you, I knew perfectly well it was locked because I did it myself after bringing the mail in at three o'clock, but I just *had* to go check it anyway. Just to be up and doing something, you know? And of course, on the way back to the living room, I noticed the picture frames in the hallway were just a fraction of an inch crooked—the ones of my grandson from his little kindergarten graduation, he looked so handsome in his tiny cap—so I had to stop and straighten those. And then I saw the hall runner was a bit bunched up, so I bent down to fix that. 

It’s just this constant, buzzing need. If I'm forced to just sit there in my chair for more than a little while, whether it's watching television or sitting in a waiting room at the dentist's office with those awful old magazines, that stirred-up sensation just builds and builds until I'm on my feet again, looking for a coaster to wipe or a window to peek out of! I just can't seem to turn that inner need off.
Do you often feel worried, anxious, or on edge about things throughout the day, even when you’re trying to relax?

Oh, no, not really. I wouldn't say I'm an anxious person, or that I feel worried or on edge. I mean, I worry about normal things, of course! Like, I worry if it's going to rain when the garden club is supposed to have our outdoor tea—Mrs. Higgins gets so cross if her hat gets damp, you wouldn't believe the fuss she made last spring when we had that unexpected drizzle. And I worry about my grandson catching a cold if he goes out without his little jacket, because you know how children are, they just run out the door without a second thought, and next thing you know they've got a sniffle that lasts for two weeks.

But that's just normal grandmother worrying, isn't it? It's not this constant, nagging anxiety or feeling like something terrible is going to happen. Even when I'm buzzing around the house and can't sit still, it's not because I'm nervous or on edge about anything in particular. It's just that physical need to move, like I was saying before. 

When I finally do sit down in the evening—usually after the dinner dishes are put away, and I've wiped down the counters, and maybe rearranged the spice rack because I couldn't find the paprika—I'm not sitting there fretting. I'm usually just thinking about what I need to do the next day, or maybe trying to remember the name of that actor in the movie I saw on Sunday. I might be physically tired, and my mind might be jumping from the grocery list to the church bake sale to whether I should finally wash the guest room curtains, but I'm not... I'm not *anxious* about it. I'm not sitting there with my heart pounding, worrying about the state of the world or anything like that. I just feel busy, I suppose. Just very, very busy, even when I'm trying to relax!
Looking back on your earlier years, would you say you were a very active or restless child who had trouble staying focused or sitting still, even when expected to?

Oh my heavens, yes. It’s funny you should ask about that, because I was just talking to my sister about this not two weeks ago. We were going through some old boxes—well, I say 'we', but I was mostly just opening them up, getting distracted by whatever was inside, and leaving her to do the actual sorting! But I actually found some of my old report cards from grade school in this lovely old cedar chest my mother used to keep at the foot of her bed. And reading through the notes on them... oh, it was just like looking in a mirror! 

Even back in grade school, my teachers always told my mother the exact same thing. They’d say I was a bright girl, very bright, but just terribly scattered. I was always, always losing my papers. I'd do my spelling homework and then somehow it would just vanish between the kitchen table and my desk at school. And the talking! Oh, I was a terrible chatterbox. I was always talking out of turn. If an idea popped into my head, it just flew right out of my mouth before I even remembered I was supposed to raise my hand. 

I remember Mrs. Gable in the third grade—she had these very thick, heavy glasses and always wore a pearl cardigan—she used to have to tap her pencil on her desk at me because I’d be wiggling and squirming in my seat, just bouncing around, and I’d be doing all that before I had even finished my work! I just couldn't wait to be done so I could see what everyone else was doing or go look out the window. My poor mother tried so hard to get me to sit properly, even at the dinner table, but I always had one knee up on the chair, ready to bolt the second I finished my peas. So, yes, I suppose that restless feeling and having trouble focusing isn't new at all. It's been with me for a very, very long time!
